items.title: Nasdaq closes above 1,000
items.summary: The Nasdaq Composite closed at 1,005.89 on 17 July 1995, its first close above 1,000.

items.title: Netscape shares reach $75 on day one
items.summary: The stock touched $75 on its first day of trading, a near record, and became the model for internet listings.
items.label: Netscape's first day

items.title: Telecoms Act signed into law
items.summary: The first big rewrite of US telecoms law in 60 years was signed on 8 February 1996, letting phone and cable firms compete.
items.label: Telecoms Act signed

items.title: Yahoo sells shares at $13 each
items.summary: Yahoo sold 2.6 million shares at $13 each on 12 April 1996; the stock closed its first day at $33.

items.title: Lucent becomes a separate company
items.summary: AT&T distributed all of its Lucent Technologies shares to its shareholders on 30 September 1996, making Lucent an independent company.

items.title: Greenspan asks about irrational exuberance
items.summary: The Federal Reserve chairman asked how we know when irrational exuberance has pushed asset values too high.
items.label: Irrational exuberance

items.title: Amazon sells shares at $18 each
items.summary: Amazon, an online bookseller, offered 3 million shares at $18 each in its first public sale.

items.title: Microsoft buys $150m of Apple shares
items.summary: At Macworld on 6 August 1997, Microsoft said it would invest $150m in Apple and keep writing Office for the Mac.
items.label: Microsoft buys Apple stake

items.title: WorldCom closes its MCI purchase
items.summary: WorldCom agreed in November 1997 to buy MCI, and the acquisition closed on 14 September 1998; WorldCom put the price at about $40bn.

items.title: Banks rescue Long-Term Capital
items.summary: On 23 September 1998, 14 banks put in $3.6bn to rescue Long-Term Capital Management, supervised by the Federal Reserve.
items.label: LTCM rescue

items.title: theGlobe.com posts the biggest first day
items.summary: theGlobe.com listed on 13 November 1998; the shares closed at $63.50, up 606% from the $9 offer price, the best first day for a company raising more than $5m.

items.title: Fed target rate falls to 4.75%
items.summary: The Federal Reserve's target rate was 4.75% on 17 November 1998, down from 6.00% in February 1995.

items.title: AOL agrees to buy Netscape
items.summary: AOL said on 24 November 1998 it would buy Netscape in a share swap valued at $4.2bn.
items.label: AOL buys Netscape

items.title: Yahoo buys GeoCities
items.summary: Yahoo acquired GeoCities in January 1999 for $3.57bn in shares, when the free web-hosting site was near the peak of the boom.

items.title: Microsoft to buy $5bn of AT&T securities
items.summary: On 6 May 1999 Microsoft agreed to pay $5bn for new AT&T convertible trust preferred securities and warrants, winning more access to AT&T's cable networks.

items.title: WorldCom worth $180bn
items.summary: WorldCom reached a market value of $180.01bn on 21 June 1999, before its long slide.

items.title: WorldCom agrees to buy Sprint
items.summary: On 5 October 1999 MCI WorldCom agreed to buy Sprint for $115bn in shares, or $129bn including debt and preferred shares.

items.title: Buffett warns of unrealistic expectations
items.summary: In a Fortune article published on 22 November 1999, Warren Buffett said investors in stocks were expecting far too much.
items.label: Buffett's Fortune warning

items.title: Lucent worth $264bn at its peak
items.summary: Lucent reached a market value of $264.50bn on 9 December 1999.

items.title: Qualcomm shares rise 2,619% in 1999
items.summary: In 1999 Qualcomm shares rose 2,619% and the Nasdaq composite 85.6%, even though more Nasdaq stocks fell than rose.

items.title: Lucent warns and the shares fall almost 30%
items.summary: On 6 January 2000 Lucent said quarterly earnings would miss estimates; the next day the shares fell 20 points, and $64bn, almost 30% of its value, went.
items.label: Lucent misses estimates

items.title: AOL agrees to merge with Time Warner
items.summary: AOL, worth about $164bn, agreed to buy Time Warner, worth about $83bn, in an all-share deal announced on 10 January 2000.
items.label: AOL buys Time Warner

items.title: Seventeen dot-coms buy Super Bowl ads
items.summary: Two dot-coms bought ads for the 1999 Super Bowl and 17 bought ads the next year, for Super Bowl XXXIV.

items.title: Global Crossing worth $49bn
items.summary: Global Crossing reached a market value of $49.12bn on 16 February 2000.

items.title: Nasdaq peaks at 5,048.62
items.summary: The Nasdaq Composite closed at 5,048.62 on 10 March 2000, the top of the boom.
items.label: Nasdaq peak

items.title: Japan recession news sparks a sell-off
items.summary: News that Japan had slipped back into recession set off a global sell-off that hit technology shares hardest.

items.title: Barron's warns internet firms are burning cash
items.summary: The Barron's cover story Burning Up said internet companies were running out of cash, and investors began to rethink.
items.label: Barron's: Burning Up

items.title: MicroStrategy restates its revenue
items.summary: MicroStrategy announced a revenue restatement and the shares fell 62% in a single day.

items.title: Cisco briefly the most valuable company
items.summary: Cisco shares reached $82, valuing the company at $569bn and briefly putting it ahead of Microsoft.

items.title: Julian Robertson closes Tiger
items.summary: Julian Robertson said on 30 March 2000 that he would close his Tiger Management fund and return outside investors' money.
items.label: Tiger fund closes

items.title: Shiller's book warns of a bubble
items.summary: Robert Shiller's book Irrational Exuberance, published in March 2000 as the Nasdaq peaked, argued that the stock market was a bubble.
items.label: Shiller's bubble book

items.title: Judge rules Microsoft broke antitrust law
items.summary: On 3 April 2000 Judge Jackson held that Microsoft had broken antitrust law by abusing its monopoly.
items.label: Microsoft loses case

items.title: Nasdaq falls 9% in one day
items.summary: The Nasdaq fell 9% on 14 April 2000, ending a week in which it lost 25%.
items.label: Nasdaq falls 9%

items.title: Fed raises its target rate to 6.50%
items.summary: On 16 May 2000 the Federal Reserve raised its target rate to 6.50%, the top of its 1999 to 2000 rises.

items.title: Qwest closes its purchase of US West
items.summary: Qwest completed its $48bn purchase of the Baby Bell US West on 30 June 2000, the first merger of a long-distance carrier and a local phone company.

items.title: Qwest worth $90bn
items.summary: Qwest reached a market value of $89.68bn on 8 August 2000.

items.title: Enron worth $67bn
items.summary: Enron reached a market value of $67.05bn on 23 August 2000.

items.title: Sun worth $205bn at its peak
items.summary: Sun Microsystems reached a market value of $205.14bn on 1 September 2000.

items.title: Pets.com goes out of business
items.summary: Pets.com, backed by Amazon and known for its sock puppet ads, said on 7 November 2000 that it would shut down and stop taking orders.

items.title: Lucent warning drags telecoms shares down
items.summary: Lucent warned of a far bigger loss than expected; the shares fell nearly 20% and had lost 80% in 2000.

items.title: Fed cuts rates between meetings
items.summary: On 3 January 2001 the Federal Reserve cut its target rate to 6.00% at a conference call, before its next meeting.

items.title: AOL Time Warner starts trading
items.summary: The AOL and Time Warner merger closed on 11 January 2001, after a year of regulatory review.
items.label: AOL Time Warner formed

items.title: eToys goes bankrupt
items.summary: The online toy seller eToys said on 26 February 2001 that it would file for bankruptcy protection and close its site on 8 March.
items.label: eToys bankrupt

items.title: Cisco warns as unsold kit piles up
items.summary: Cisco warned sales would fall, took a $4bn charge, cut a fifth of its jobs and was worth under $100bn.

items.title: JDS Uniphase posts a $50.6bn loss
items.summary: JDS Uniphase lost $50.6bn in the year to June after writing down acquisitions, and planned 16,000 job cuts.

items.title: Attacks close the markets and speed the fall
items.summary: The 11 September attacks closed the stock exchanges until 17 September and deepened the market fall that began in 2000.
items.label: 9/11 closes markets

items.title: Nortel cuts 20,000 more jobs
items.summary: Nortel warned of a $3.6bn quarterly loss, cut 20,000 jobs and named Frank Dunn chief executive.

items.title: Enron files for bankruptcy
items.summary: Enron filed for bankruptcy on 2 December 2001, then the largest in US history, after fraud was revealed.
items.label: Enron bankrupt

items.title: Global Crossing files for bankruptcy
items.summary: Global Crossing filed for Chapter 11 with $22.4bn of assets and $12.4bn of debts; the shares had fallen 96% in a year.

items.title: WorldCom admits $3.9bn of improper entries
items.summary: On 25 June 2002 WorldCom said it would restate its accounts after finding $3.055bn of improper transfers in 2001 and $797m more in early 2002.
items.label: WorldCom fraud revealed

items.title: WorldCom heads into the biggest bankruptcy
items.summary: WorldCom said on 21 July 2002 it would file for Chapter 11 with $104bn of assets, a month after admitting fraud.

items.title: Sarbanes-Oxley signed into law
items.summary: President Bush signed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act on 30 July 2002, tightening company accounts after the scandals.
items.label: Sarbanes-Oxley signed

items.title: Nasdaq closes at a six-year low
items.summary: On 9 October 2002 the Nasdaq composite closed at 1,114.11, a six-year low; the Wilshire 5000 was 50% below its March 2000 high, with $8.5tn gone.
items.label: Nasdaq bottom
